study_identification.author_journal_year: Coupé et al., Human Brain Mapping, 2022
study_identification.title: Hippocampal-amygdalo-ventricular atrophy score: Alzheimer disease detection using normative and pathological lifespan models

clarity_of_research_objectives.reason: The paper clearly states its research objectives in multiple locations. The abstract explicitly states the purpose: 'present an innovative MRI-based method for Alzheimer disease (AD) detection and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) prognostic, using lifespan trajectories of brain structures.' The introduction describes proposing 'a novel method able to detect patients with AD using both normal and pathological lifespan models.' The PICO elements are identifiable: Population (AD patients, MCI, CN subjects), Intervention (normative modeling with HAVAs), Comparator (normative modeling, classical ML, deep learning methods), and Outcome (diagnostic accuracy, prognostic capability). The specific application purpose is clearly stated as diagnostic support and prognosis.
clarity_of_research_objectives.supporting_text: In this article, we present an innovative MRI-based method for Alzheimer disease (AD) detection and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) prognostic, using lifespan trajectories of brain structures; we present an alternative framework combining advantages of both strategies: an easy interpretation and an accurate classification

clear_definition_of_target_population.reason: The paper provides demographic characteristics (age, sex, sample sizes) for all groups in Tables 1 and 2. However, diagnostic criteria for AD are not explicitly specified. The paper does not mention DSM-5, ICD-11, or any specific diagnostic criteria. For MCI classification, the paper states 'we used the ClinicaDL software to define the groups of AD and CN groups in AIBL, and the pMCI and sMCI groups in ADNI. Therefore, we used the same selection criteria' but does not detail what those criteria are. The definition of healthy control groups is described only as 'cognitively normal (CN) subjects' without further specification.
clear_definition_of_target_population.supporting_text: This dataset was composed of 2,655 CN subjects (CN) and 377 patients with AD; we used the ClinicaDL software (https://github.com/aramis-lab/clinicadl) (Wen et al., 2020) to define the groups of AD and CN groups in AIBL, and the pMCI and sMCI groups in ADNI

clarity_of_inclusion_and_exclusion_crite.reason: The paper mentions quality control procedures but does not provide clear, pre-specified inclusion and exclusion criteria uniformly applied to all participants. Quality control is mentioned: 'For all the training subjects detected as failure by the automatic QC RegQCNet, a visual assessment was performed by individually checking the input images and the segmentations produced by AssemblyNet using a 3D viewer. If the failure was confirmed by our expert, the subject was removed from training dataset.' However, specific clinical inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., comorbidities, medication use, cognitive score thresholds) are not described. The paper does not include a flow chart showing subject numbers at each stage, nor does it specify the number of subjects excluded or reasons for exclusion beyond QC failures.
clarity_of_inclusion_and_exclusion_crite.supporting_text: For all the training subjects detected as failure by the automatic QC RegQCNet (Denis de Senneville et al., 2020), a visual assessment was performed by individually checking the input images and the segmentations produced by AssemblyNet using a 3D viewer. If the failure was confirmed by our expert, the subject was removed from training dataset

validity_of_normative_modeling_outcome_m.reason: The paper clearly defines brain measures used (hippocampus, amygdala, inferior lateral ventricle volumes) and describes methods for quantifying individual-level deviations in detail. The normative reference population is well-specified: 'For CN trajectories, we used the N = 2,655 subjects from 9 months to 94y of the training dataset.' The AD trajectory construction is also clearly described: 'we used N = 2,251 subjects...we used 377 AD patients (from 55y to 96y) and all the CN younger than 55y available in the training dataset (i.e., 1874 subjects).' Interpretation methods for deviation scores are clearly explained with mathematical formulas and the HAVAs score is described as 'reflects the probability for the subject under study to be a patient with AD.'
validity_of_normative_modeling_outcome_m.supporting_text: To create our lifespan models, we estimated normal and pathological trajectories of structure volumes across the entire lifespan. To this end, for each considered structure, models were estimated on two different groups to generate CN and AD trajectories. For CN trajectories, we used the N = 2,655 subjects from 9 months to 94y of the training dataset as done in Coupé et al. (2017). For the AD trajectories, we used N = 2,251 subjects; Consequently, the proposed HAVAs (i.e., the S AD score) reflects the probability for the subject under study to be a patient with AD (or a pMCI subject)

handling_of_confounding_variables.reason: The paper addresses age and intracranial volume (ICV) normalization but does not explicitly describe handling of sex as a covariate in the models. Age is central to the lifespan modeling approach. ICV normalization is described: 'To compensate for the inter-subject variability, we normalized all the structure volumes using the intracranial cavity volume (ICV).' The data comes from multiple sites (7 databases for training, additional databases for testing), but there is no explicit discussion of how site effects are handled beyond the normalization procedure. The paper does not describe harmonization methods (e.g., ComBat) for multi-site data. Sex is recorded in the demographic tables but there is no mention of sex-specific models or sex as a covariate in the polynomial models.
handling_of_confounding_variables.supporting_text: To compensate for the inter-subject variability, we normalized all the structure volumes using the intracranial cavity volume (ICV) (Manjón et al., 2014). Moreover, in order to be able to combine several structures with different sizes, we performed z-score normalization of all the normalized volumes (in percentage of ICV)

details_of_data_preprocessing.reason: The preprocessing procedures are clearly and comprehensively described. The paper specifies the software used (AssemblyNet) and details each preprocessing step: 'The AssemblyNet preprocessing pipeline was based on several steps: image denoising, inhomogeneity correction, affine registration to the MNI space, automatic quality control (QC), a second inhomogeneity correction in the MNI space and a final intensity standardization step.' Segmentation procedures are described with reference to protocols (Neuromorphometrics protocol, 132 structures). Quality control procedures are detailed: both automatic QC (RegQCNet) and visual inspection by experts. The paper also provides a software repository (https://github.com/volBrain/AssemblyNet).

clarity_of_data_partitioning_methods.reason: The paper does not describe data partitioning into training, validation, and test sets in the traditional machine learning sense. While the paper clearly distinguishes between training datasets (ADNI, OASIS, C-MIND, NDAR, ABIDE, ICBM, IXI) and external testing datasets (AIBL, MIRIAD, ADNI-MCI), there is no mention of a separate validation set used during model development. The paper does not specify data partition ratios, partitioning methods (random, stratified), or use of cross-validation. The lifespan models are fitted directly to the training data using polynomial regression with model selection based on statistical criteria (F-statistic, T-statistic, BIC) rather than performance on a held-out validation set.
clarity_of_data_partitioning_methods.supporting_text: we performed a screening to detect the most discriminant ones in terms of classification accuracy on the training ADNI dataset in order not to use testing data during method development

details_of_normative_modeling_approach.reason: The statistical approaches used for normative modeling are described in detail. The paper specifies the types of models considered (linear, quadratic, and cubic polynomial models) with mathematical formulas. Model selection criteria are clearly described: 'a polynomial model was considered as a potential candidate only when simultaneously F-statistic based on ANOVA (i.e., model vs. constant model) was found significant (p < .05) and when all its coefficients were also significant using T-statistic (p < .05). Afterwards, to select the most relevant model between these potential candidates, we used the Bayesian Information Criterion.' The software used is specified (AssemblyNet). Volume normalization procedures are detailed (ICV normalization and z-score normalization).
details_of_normative_modeling_approach.supporting_text: To estimate the volume trajectories, we considered several low order polynomial models: Linear model, Quadratic model, Cubic model; a polynomial model was considered as a potential candidate only when simultaneously F-statistic based on ANOVA (i.e., model vs. constant model) was found significant (p < .05) and when all its coefficients were also significant using T-statistic (p < .05). Afterwards, to select the most relevant model between these potential candidates, we used the Bayesian Information Criterion (Schwarz, 1978)

No optimization algorithms (gradient descent, ADAM, L-BFGS) are mentioned. No hyperparameter setting methods (grid search, Bayesian optimization) are described beyond the model selection using statistical criteria (F-test, T-test, BIC). There are no convergence criteria or training termination conditions because the polynomial models are fitted analytically. Regularization techniques (L1/L2 regularization) are not mentioned. This is appropriate for the polynomial regression approach used, but means these details are inherently not applicable for this type of model.

external_data_validation.reason: The paper conducts extensive external validation on multiple independent datasets. Testing is performed on AIBL (467 CN/82 AD), MIRIAD (23 CN/46 AD), and ADNI-MCI (255 sMCI/235 pMCI) datasets that were not used for training (Table 5). The characteristics of these external validation datasets are described in Table 2 with demographic information (sample sizes, age, sex distribution). Performance on external validation is thoroughly reported and compared with internal training results. The paper also includes a sensitivity analysis where they swap training and testing datasets: 'using AIBL, OASIS, and MIRIAD databases in the training dataset while removing the AD and CN subjects of the ADNI database from training and used them as testing dataset.' This demonstrates robustness to domain shift and generalization capability across different datasets.

additional_comments.additional_comments: 1. Methodological Innovation: This paper presents an interesting hybrid approach that uses both normal (CN) and pathological (AD) lifespan models for classification, which differs from traditional normative modeling that uses only the normal model. This dual-model approach appears to improve classification accuracy. 2. Multi-site Data Without Explicit Harmonization: The study uses data from 7 different databases with potentially different acquisition protocols but does not explicitly describe harmonization methods (e.g., ComBat, traveling subjects). The reliance on ICV normalization and z-score standardization may not fully address scanner/site differences, particularly for multi-site normative modeling where these effects can be substantial. 3. Limited Clinical Characterization: While the paper provides excellent demographic data, it lacks clinical characterization of the patient populations (symptom severity, illness duration, medication status, comorbidities). For MCI subjects, prognostic information (conversion timeframe) is provided but baseline cognitive measures are not. 4. Feature Selection Using Training Data: The paper acknowledges using the training ADNI dataset to screen for the most discriminant structures, which could introduce some optimism bias. However, the extensive external validation on completely independent datasets (AIBL, MIRIAD) and the sensitivity analysis using different training/testing splits suggest the results are robust. 5. Polynomial Models vs. More Flexible Approaches: The use of low-order polynomial models (linear, quadratic, cubic) is appropriate for lifespan modeling and provides interpretability. However, more flexible approaches (e.g., GAM, GAMLSS, splines) that could capture non-linearities or heteroscedasticity across the lifespan are not explored or compared. 6. Clinical Utility vs. Technical Performance: The paper makes a strong case for clinical utility through interpretability and simplicity, which is valuable. The comparison with deep learning methods is well-designed and addresses the important issue of overfitting and generalization in the AD classification literature. 7. Age Range Consideration: The training data spans from 9 months to 96 years, providing excellent lifespan coverage. However, the testing for AD is focused on older adults (55-96y), which is appropriate for the disease but means the younger age models are less validated for AD detection. 8. MCI Prognosis Without Training on MCI: The paper demonstrates that models trained only on AD and CN subjects can discriminate between stable and progressive MCI (78% AUC), which is a strength showing generalization to related but unseen tasks. 9. Reproducibility Strengths: The commitment to making code, software, and online tools available (volBrain platform, Docker containers, GitHub repositories) is commendable and supports reproducibility. The use of publicly available datasets also facilitates replication. 10. This assessment has been conducted conservatively according to the guidelines, marking items as 'Partial' or 'No' when information is unclear, incomplete, or missing, even when the overall study quality may be reasonable for the research question addressed.
